report:
I researched this, and the evidence actually contradicts the assumption that olive leaf extract has no effect on blood pressure — most credible clinical evidence suggests it *does* have a modest antihypertensive effect, at least at higher doses.

The strongest piece of evidence is a randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial in patients with stage-1 hypertension, published in *Phytomedicine* (Susalit et al., 2011). It found that olive leaf extract (EFLA®943, 500 mg twice daily) lowered systolic and diastolic blood pressure similarly to captopril, a standard ACE-inhibitor drug (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0944711310002709). This is a fairly rigorous, peer-reviewed RCT and is the most reliable evidence available here.

A synthesis from Examine.com, a research-aggregation site known for evidence-based summaries, similarly concludes that olive leaf extract, rich in oleuropein, "may help reduce blood pressure and improve blood lipids" (https://examine.com/supplements/olive-leaf-extract/research/).

Other sources in the search results (blogs, supplement marketing sites) repeat similar claims, but they are lower quality, often citing the same trial or making unsubstantiated assertions without primary data.

**Conclusion:** Based on the available evidence, the answer to "Can olive leaf extract reduce high blood pressure?" appears to be **yes, modestly**, not "no." The main supporting evidence is one solid RCT showing effects comparable to a low-dose ACE inhibitor in stage-1 hypertension, corroborated by an independent research review. However, evidence is limited to a small number of trials, so confidence should remain moderate rather than definitive, and larger independent replications would strengthen the case.
